transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, to be honest, it took a lot for me to actually make this appointment. I mean, I'm on the road a lot, right? I've been driving a rig and making deliveries for, gosh, almost thirty years now, straight out of high school, and I've always prided myself on running a really tight ship. My routes, my logs, keeping the customers happy—I've always been the guy who remembers every little thing. But lately... well, what finally got me in here is that over these past few months, my mind just won't stay put. 

It’s like I’m behind the wheel, and instead of just focusing on the road and the job, my brain keeps jumping to absolutely everything else. Every single time the CB radio chirps, I'm completely derailed. Or I'll be driving down the interstate and see a fuel price sign at a truck stop, and suddenly I'm doing all this math in my head about profit margins and coming up with these massive new ideas for how the company should be routing our freight. Just boom, boom, boom, onto the next thought. 

And because my head is bouncing around like a pinball, I'm missing details. Details I normally never, ever miss. Like last week, I completely blew past a client’s delivery note about where exactly to drop their pallets, which caused a huge headache for the receiving guys on the dock. Or I'll completely forget who I promised to call back. I'll tell my dispatcher or my wife I'll call them in ten minutes, I'll have the phone right there on the dash, and then I get distracted by some new idea and completely ghost them. It’s just getting to the point where I can't keep dropping the ball like this, you know?
Are you noticing any difficulties or distractions like this when you're not working, like when you're at home with your family?

Yeah, yeah, it's definitely happening at home, too, which is... honestly, it's really tough to admit. You know, I come off the road, and I'm supposed to be present, right? I'm supposed to be the guy who fixes the leaky faucet and helps out, but lately... man. I'll walk into the house, and instead of just sitting down and asking my wife how her day was, I'm suddenly obsessed with reorganizing the entire garage because I had this thought on the drive back about maximizing storage efficiency. And then half an hour later, I'm out there pulling everything off the shelves, making a huge mess, and my wife is just... she's standing there, looking at me like I've lost my mind. 

It's gotten to the point where she and my daughter, who's a senior in high school and already stressed enough with college applications and all that, they're just walking on eggshells around me. I can see it in their faces. They don't want to set me off on another tangent or interrupt whatever grand plan I'm cooking up in my head. I'm supposed to be helping them, easing the load, but I know I'm just adding strain. 

And it's not just at home, either. I know I mentioned the driving, but even with the sales side of things—because I do some sales follow-ups for the routes, too—it's bleeding into that. Just last week, I had to ask dispatch to repeat the same load instructions three times. Three times! And a couple of my regular clients, guys I've known for years, I completely forgot to do their follow-up calls because I was chasing down some wild idea about overhauling our entire regional delivery schedule. I was so wrapped up in this massive plan that I let the basic stuff, the stuff that actually pays the bills, just slip right through the cracks. It's like I'm trying to juggle twenty balls at once, and I'm dropping the most important ones, both at work and sitting right there in my own living room.
Are you feeling like your difficulties with focusing and staying on task are affecting your relationships with your family or your job performance?

Well, yeah, exactly. That's... I mean, that's exactly what I'm trying to say, doc. That's the whole reason I finally picked up the phone to make this appointment, which, like I said, is not something I'd normally do. Because, normally, I'm the guy everyone relies on. You know? I've been married to my wife for twenty-some years, and she's always known me as the steady one. The guy who brings home the paycheck, keeps the trucks running on time, makes sure the yard is mowed and the house is in order. 

And now, I'm just... I feel like a tornado tearing through my own life. It really eats at me, sitting in the cab of my truck, realizing I just let down a guy on the dock who I've known since the late nineties. Because in this business, relationships are absolutely everything. You lose a client's trust because you were too busy daydreaming about some pie-in-the-sky logistics overhaul to remember their specific instructions, and well, word gets around. The trucking industry is a lot smaller than you think. 

And with my daughter, like I was saying, it just breaks my heart. She's got her college tours and all this pressure on her shoulders, and instead of being her rock, I'm out in the garage making a racket with my tools or pacing around because I can't just sit still and watch a movie with them for one single evening. So, yes, absolutely, it's affecting everything. It's like I'm watching myself mess up the dynamic with my family and my reputation at my job, and I just can't seem to pump the brakes. I just want to get back to being the guy who remembers to make his follow-up calls and can actually sit at the dinner table without his mind racing a million miles a minute, you know?
Do you feel restless or fidgety when you're not able to act on these thoughts or ideas that are distracting you?

Oh, restless doesn't even begin to cover it, doc. It's like... it's like I've got this motor humming inside me, right in my chest, and if I don't give it somewhere to go, I just about crawl out of my skin. I mean, I've always been a hard worker, you don't survive thirty years in trucking if you're lazy, but lately, it's just non-stop. I can't just finish my shift, park the rig, and call it a day. I keep finding all these extra jobs for myself. 

Like, the other night, I get home, right? It's been a twelve-hour day, I should be exhausted, I should be putting my feet up with a cold beer. But instead, I'm sitting at the kitchen table until two in the morning, completely rewriting these route plans for the entire regional fleet, which isn't even my job, mind you. But I just had to do it. And then I'm calling up the new drivers, these young kids who just got their CDLs, checking in on them way after hours, giving them tips on how to handle the mountain passes, just talking their ears off because I have to be doing something. 

And if I'm not doing that, I'm finding things to fix around the house. I mentioned the garage earlier, but it's the gutters, it's the weatherstripping on the back door, it's taking apart the lawnmower engine just to see if I can make it run a little leaner. If I try to just sit on the couch with my wife to watch a show, my leg starts bouncing. Tap, tap, tap, tap. And I get this tight, antsy feeling, like I'm wasting time, like there's a million things I'm supposed to be doing and if I don't get up right that second and do them, I'm going to explode. I just... I physically cannot sit still for more than five minutes without feeling like I need to jump up and tackle another project.
Are you feeling like you're at risk of losing your job due to these difficulties with focusing and staying on task?

Well, that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? I mean, I've got thirty years of goodwill built up with this company, so they're not gonna just hand me a pink slip tomorrow, but... yeah, I'm scared. I really am. Because like I was telling you a minute ago, at work, I’ve had to have dispatch and even my clients repeat details that I absolutely should have tracked the first time. I'm the veteran, I'm supposed to be the sharp one, and here I am asking them to repeat basic instructions over and over. It's humiliating, honestly. 

And a couple of my important sales follow-ups just completely slipped through because I was chasing too many ideas at once. My brain is just bouncing from one grand scheme to the next, trying to reinvent the wheel, and the actual work—the stuff that keeps me employed and keeps the lights on—is suffering. If I keep dropping the ball with clients and messing up the logistics, my seniority isn't gonna save me forever. The boss is gonna have to step in eventually if I keep costing them money or making us look bad.

And honestly, doc, it's the exact same story when I pull into my driveway. I know I mentioned them earlier, but at home, my wife and daughter have just been walking on eggshells around me. I can see the look in their eyes when I walk through the door, like they're trying to gauge what mood I'm in or what crazy project I'm about to tear into next. I can tell I’m adding all this extra strain when I’m supposed to be helping them. My daughter needs a dad who can help her look at college brochures, not a dad who is tearing the lawnmower apart at midnight. It just feels like everything I touch right now, whether it's my route sheet or my own family, I'm just making a mess of it because I can't keep my head straight.
Are you feeling like these difficulties are significantly impacting your ability to enjoy your daily life or maintain your relationships?

Yeah, doc, like I was just saying a second ago, it's really taking a massive toll on everything. Enjoying my life? I don't even know what that means right now, to be perfectly honest with you. It's exactly like I was just telling you about the job—it's getting to the point where I'm constantly having to ask dispatch to run through the route details again, or I'm on the phone with a long-time client and I have to say, 'Hey, sorry, can you repeat that?' because my brain was off chasing a hundred different ideas at once instead of tracking what I should have been tracking. And those sales follow-ups I mentioned that just slipped right through the cracks? That's not just a minor hiccup, that's my livelihood, and it completely ruins my day because I'm just sick with stress about dropping the ball when I know better. 

And as for maintaining my relationships... well, I touched on this just a minute ago, but it's really hitting me hard. My wife and my daughter, they're the most important people in the world to me, and right now, they're just tiptoeing around the house. They're walking on eggshells every single day because they don't know what version of me is coming through that front door. I'm supposed to be the guy they lean on. I'm supposed to be helping them, especially with my daughter trying to figure out her future, being that solid foundation for her. And instead, I can just see it in their faces that I'm adding all this extra strain to their lives. It just breaks my heart. So, yeah, "impacting" is probably putting it lightly. It feels like it's completely turning my daily life and my family relationships upside down, and I just can't seem to fix it.
Are you experiencing these difficulties with focusing and staying on task at the same level all the time, or are there specific times of the day or situations when they seem worse?

Well, it's funny you ask about the timing, because it's... it's really when I'm in the cab of the truck, mostly, or when there's just a lot of stimulus going on around me. Though honestly, it feels like it's just been this constant, exhausting hum these past few months. 

Like, I'll be driving down I-80, right? A route I've done a thousand times, I could drive it blindfolded. Usually, I'm laser-focused, just watching the traffic, feeling the rhythm of the road. But lately... man, lately, it's like every single little thing pulls my brain in a completely different direction. The CB radio will chirp—just a quick squawk, you know, maybe somebody calling out a speed trap or a backup near the weigh station—and suddenly my mind is racing about a dozen different things, trying to redesign the whole communication protocol for our dispatch. Or I'll pass a travel center, and I see the fuel price sign lit up, and instead of just noting it like a normal driver, I'm suddenly doing all this crazy math in my head about the entire regional fleet's fuel consumption and how we could restructure our vendor contracts to save pennies on the gallon. 

And while my brain is off chasing every new idea that pops into my head, the actual work just falls right out of my brain. Honestly, doc, that is what finally got me in here to see you. Because over these months, my mind just keeps jumping to every CB chirp, every fuel price sign, or every grand new idea, and I end up missing details I normally never, ever miss. I've been doing this thirty years, I pride myself on being sharp, but I'll get to a loading dock and realize I completely glossed over a client’s delivery note about which specific bay they needed the pallets in, or I'll look at the clock and realize it's five in the evening and I have absolutely no idea who I promised to call back for a sales follow-up. 

So I guess to answer your question, it's happening all day, but it really flares up the worst when I'm out there on the road, surrounded by all those little things that just hijack my attention and send me down a rabbit hole while the important stuff just completely evaporates from my memory.
Do you feel like these difficulties are making it hard for you to do your job or affect your relationships with others?

Well, doc, I feel like a bit of a broken record here since we just went over this, but yes, it absolutely is. I mean, it's doing exactly that. Like I was telling you a few minutes ago, it's making things incredibly difficult on both fronts. 

At work, it’s just embarrassing. You spend thirty years building a reputation as the reliable guy, the one who never misses a beat, and now? Now I’ve had to have dispatch, and even worse, my actual clients, repeat details that I absolutely should have tracked the first time around. I'm sitting there on the phone or the radio, nodding along, but nothing is sticking. And then there are those sales follow-ups I mentioned. A couple of really good ones just slipped right through the cracks completely, all because I was busy chasing too many ideas at once. My brain is off trying to reinvent our whole routing system, and meanwhile, the actual guy waiting for a call back about a delivery is just left hanging. It makes doing my job near impossible some days when I can't even hold onto a basic instruction.

And then I clock out, and the exact same problem follows me right through my front door. Like I said before, my relationships are taking a huge hit. At home, my wife and daughter have just been walking on eggshells around me. You have no idea how much it hurts a man's pride to see his own family tiptoeing around the living room, trying to figure out what kind of mood he's in or what wild tangent he's gonna go off on next. I can see it in their faces, the way their shoulders tense up. I can tell I’m adding all this heavy strain to their lives, and the worst part is, I’m supposed to be the one helping them. I'm supposed to be the rock, especially for my daughter right now, and instead, I'm just this whirlwind making everything harder for everyone. So, yeah, it's definitely affecting my job and my family, and I just don't know how to hit the brakes on it.
Are there any times of the day when you feel more in control of your thoughts and able to focus?

Well, doc, you know, I've really been trying to figure that out myself, because you'd think there'd be some sort of pattern, right? Like, maybe first thing in the morning when I've just had my coffee, sitting at the kitchen table before the sun comes up. I've always been an early riser, usually up by 4:00 AM, enjoying the quiet before the house wakes up. You'd think that would be the time my brain is clear. But honestly? No. I sit there with my mug, and instead of just enjoying the silence, my brain is already running a million miles an hour, cataloging every single thing I need to do for the week, or coming up with some grand scheme to reorganize the garage that I absolutely have to start right that second, even though it's pitch black outside. 

And then you'd think, okay, maybe at the end of the day, right? When the truck is parked, the paperwork is done, and I'm just sitting in my recliner watching the evening news. But even then, I'm not really watching the news. The anchor is talking about the weather, and I'm suddenly obsessing over how the barometric pressure is going to affect tire wear on the fleet, and before I know it, I've got my notebook out and I'm scribbling down calculations while my wife is trying to ask me what I want for dinner. 

So, I don't know, to answer your question... I haven't really found a time where I feel like I'm holding the steering wheel, so to speak. It just feels like this constant, buzzing engine in my head that won't idle down, morning, noon, or night. I keep hoping I'll find that pocket of time where things just settle, where I can just focus on one thing at a time without feeling like I'm juggling chainsaws, but so far... I just haven't noticed any specific time of day where I feel more in control. It's just all the time.
Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking through the consequences of your actions?

Well... no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, it's a fair question, doc, considering how much I just told you about my brain bouncing around like a pinball in a machine, but... see, there's a big difference between what my brain is doing and what I actually *do* in the real world. 

My thoughts? Sure, they're all over the place. But my actions? I've always been a measure-twice, cut-once kind of guy, and even with all this... this exhausting noise in my head these past few months, I haven't lost that. Like, take the driving, for instance. I might be sitting in the cab obsessing over how to completely redesign our dispatch software, but I'm not suddenly gonna yank the steering wheel and take an exit I'm not supposed to take just because the urge struck me. Or with the business side of things—I might have a dozen wild ideas about restructuring our fuel vendor contracts, like I mentioned earlier, but I'm not actually picking up the phone and firing our suppliers on a whim without running the numbers. 

I guess what I'm trying to say is, the engine in my head is revving way, way too high, but I still have my foot firmly on the brake when it comes to actually making a move. I'm not going out and making rash decisions that I can't take back, or doing anything crazy like that. My wife, bless her heart, she’s stressed to the gills about my moods and my tangents right now, but she knows I'm not a reckless man. I've always taken my responsibilities to my family and my job incredibly seriously. You spend thirty years hauling freight, you learn real quick that acting without thinking is what gets people hurt, or gets your CDL pulled. 

So, even when my brain is practically screaming at me to chase down some grand new scheme right this very second, I don't actually pull the trigger on it. I don't act on it. I just... I just completely exhaust myself thinking about it, if that makes sense.
Are you feeling like these difficulties are significantly impacting your overall well-being or daily functioning?

Well, doc, I know we kind of just touched on this a few minutes ago when you asked about my job and my family, but... yeah, it really, really is taking a massive toll on my overall well-being. I mean, when you look at my daily functioning, it's just a mess compared to how I usually operate, and it eats at me. 

Going back to what I was saying about work—it’s not just that it’s hard, it’s how it makes me feel about myself. Sitting in that cab, having to key the radio and ask dispatch to repeat a simple gate code or delivery instruction that I absolutely should have tracked the first time... it makes a guy feel incompetent. I’ve been driving and selling for a long time, and having clients repeat themselves because I was zoning out? That’s just not me. And those sales follow-ups I mentioned slipping through the cracks? That’s money off the table. That’s my livelihood taking a hit just because my brain was too busy chasing a dozen different ideas at once instead of just making a simple five-minute phone call. It’s incredibly frustrating to know you're capable of doing the work, but your brain just refuses to line up and do it. 

And as for my well-being at home... man, that’s the part that really keeps me up, even more than the racing thoughts. Like I brought up earlier, my wife and daughter have been walking on eggshells around me, and living in a house like that... it’s heavy. You walk through your own front door and you can just feel the air shift. It gets tense. I see them exchanging these looks, trying to gauge where my head is at, wondering if I'm gonna start pacing a hole in the carpet or launching into some huge speech about a new project. It breaks my heart, honestly. I'm a family man. I'm supposed to be the one helping them, the one taking the weight off their shoulders, and instead, I can tell I’m just adding all this unnecessary strain to their daily lives. 

So, yeah, to answer your question... it's impacting everything. It’s exhausting trying to function like this day in and day out, feeling like I'm letting people down left and right.
Do you find yourself interrupting others frequently or finishing their sentences for them?

Well, no, not really. I mean, it’s a good question, considering how much I’ve been talking your ear off today, and how fast everything is moving upstairs. You’d probably expect me to be jumping all over people’s words, right? But honestly, I don't really do that. 

See, in my line of work—especially on the sales side of things, but even just dealing with dispatch or the guys on the loading docks—you learn pretty early on that you have to let the other guy finish his thought. If I’m sitting across from a warehouse manager, trying to get him to commit to a new freight contract, and I start cutting him off or finishing his sentences? He’s gonna think I’m a pushy jerk, and I’m gonna lose the account right then and there. So over the last thirty years, I’ve built up this... this deeply ingrained habit of just keeping my mouth shut and nodding until it’s my turn to speak, no matter how antsy I'm feeling. 

And at home, with my wife... well, like I was saying earlier about how I zone out? That’s usually what happens instead. If she’s telling me about her day at work, or talking about her sister’s kids, I’m not jumping in to finish her sentences because, frankly, doc, half the time I have absolutely no idea what she’s about to say anyway. My mind is already three states away, trying to calculate diesel costs or obsessing over that dispatch software I mentioned. So I just kind of sit there in my recliner, quiet on the outside, while the engine is just roaring on the inside. 

I’m definitely not a great listener right now, I'll be the first to admit that. And I might take a second too long to respond when someone finally does stop talking, because I have to sort of snap myself back to reality and figure out what we were even talking about. But I'm not actively talking over anyone or cutting them off. I just... I let them talk, even if I'm not really hearing it the way I should be.
Do you find yourself often making careless mistakes or failing to follow through on instructions?

Yeah... yeah, that’s actually... well, to be perfectly honest with you, doc, that’s exactly what finally got me to come in here and sit in that chair. That right there. Because I can handle feeling a little wired, you know? But the mistakes? That messes with my livelihood, and I just can't have that. 

Over these last few months, it’s like... it’s like my brain has absolutely no filter anymore. I'll be rolling down the interstate, right? And normally, I'm locked in. I know my route, I know my rig, I know my clients. But lately, my mind just keeps jumping to every single little thing around me. Every time the CB chirps, I completely lose my train of thought. I'll drive past a truck stop and see a fuel price sign, and instead of just noting it and keeping my eyes on the road, my brain goes off on this massive, hour-long tangent about national diesel averages, or I get completely swept up in some brand new idea for restructuring our sales routes. 

And because my head is just constantly bouncing around from one shiny object to the next, I'm dropping the ball on the actual job. I'm missing details that I normally never, ever miss. I've been doing this for thirty years, I don't make rookie mistakes. But suddenly, I'm looking right at a client's delivery note and I just completely gloss over the gate code, or I miss the specific loading dock they told me to back into. Or, like I was saying earlier about the sales side—I'll talk to a guy, tell him, "Hey, let me check the freight schedule and call you right back," and... poof. The thought is just gone. Completely erased. 

It’s not because I don't care, it’s because by the time I reach for my phone to make that call, I’ve already been distracted by three other things. A weird sound in the engine, a billboard, a new pitch I want to try... it’s just exhausting. Do you know how embarrassing it is to have a client call you up three hours later asking where their quote is, and you have to make up some excuse about bad cell service because you can't admit you just completely forgot you promised to call them back? It’s not like me at all. I pride myself on follow-through. If I say I'm gonna do something, I do it. But these past few months, it's like I can't hold onto a thought long enough to follow a simple instruction before something else catches my eye or my ear, and it's driving me absolutely crazy.
Do you often feel a strong need to be constantly active, even when it's not necessary?

Oh, absolutely. It’s like my motor is just idling way too high, and if I don't put it in gear, I'm gonna overheat. I just can't seem to stop moving lately. 

If I try to just sit still for more than five minutes—like if I try to just sit in my recliner and watch a ballgame like a normal guy—my skin practically starts crawling. I get so unbelievably antsy. So to deal with it, I just keep finding all these extra jobs for myself, even when I'm technically off the clock and supposed to be resting. 

Like the other night, for example. Instead of just relaxing with my wife, I was up at the kitchen table for God knows how long, completely rewriting our regional route plans. And the thing is, our dispatch software already does that automatically, right? It optimizes everything. But I just convinced myself that the computer was missing things, and that I could shave off a few miles or avoid some nasty intersections if I just mapped the whole grid out by hand. So there I am, papers everywhere, drawing lines all over the place. 

And then when I finally put that away, I’m pulling out my phone and checking on the new drivers after hours. I'll call up the rookies at eight or nine at night just to see if they have any questions about their pre-trip inspections for the next morning, or if they need advice on securing a weird load. I mean, they probably think I'm some crazy micromanager breathing down their necks, but I just can't shut the work side of my brain off. I have to be doing something productive. 

And it’s not just work, either. If I’m not messing with trucking stuff, I’m finding things to fix around the house. Well, I say fixing, but half the time I'm messing with things that barely even need it. Just this past weekend, I completely took apart the track on the garage door just because it squeaked a little bit when it rolled up. And then as soon as I put that back together, I decided the back deck absolutely had to be power-washed right then and there. My wife is standing in the kitchen window, just looking at me like I've lost my mind, begging me to just come inside and drink a cup of coffee with her. But I just... I can't do it, doc. If I sit down, that antsy, restless feeling just bubbles right back up in my chest, and I have to go find the next project just to burn off the energy. It’s exhausting, but I just can't stop doing it.
Do you often find yourself starting a task before you've finished the previous one?

Well, no, not really. I know I just sat here and told you how distracted I get, and how I'll forget to call a client back because something else caught my eye, but... that's a little different than actually starting a job and leaving it half-done. If I actually get my hands dirty and start a project, I see it through. I don't just drop my tools and walk away to do something else. 

Like that garage door track I was just telling you about? I didn't stop halfway through loosening the brackets to go, I don't know, mow the front lawn or something. I stayed right there on that stepladder until the whole track was perfectly aligned, greased up, and bolted back tight. Same with the power-washing. I didn't just do three boards on the deck and decide to go clean the gutters instead. I stood out there for two hours and blasted every single square inch of that wood until it looked brand new. 

I think a lot of that comes from being on the road for so long. When you're driving a rig, or even just managing a fleet, you can't just stop halfway through a process. You can't do half a pre-trip inspection, check the tires and the brakes, and then suddenly decide to go organize your logbook instead of checking the airlines, you know? If you do that, you end up failing a DOT inspection at the weigh station, or worse, you end up in a ditch. So I have this deeply ingrained rule that if I start a physical task, I finish it. A to Z. 

So, yeah, my brain might be moving a million miles an hour, and I might be thinking about the next five projects I want to tackle while I'm working on the current one... but my hands stay on the job in front of me. I might rush through it because I'm so eager to get to the next thing, but I don't abandon it in the middle. That's just sloppy, and like I said, I pride myself on not doing sloppy work. I mean, if my old man had ever caught me leaving a chore half-finished when I was a kid, he would've... well, anyway. No, I don't really leave things unfinished to start new ones. I just line them all up and knock them down one by one.
Do you find yourself having trouble focusing or paying attention in quiet environments, like when you're reading a book or working on a puzzle?

Quiet environments? Puzzles? Well, to be perfectly honest with you, I haven't sat down to do a jigsaw puzzle in probably twenty years. My wife, she loves those thousand-piece landscape ones, sets them up on the card table in the corner, but I just don't have the patience for that kind of thing right now. But as far as reading a book or just trying to focus when it's quiet? Oh, forget about it. It’s absolutely impossible lately. 

It’s exactly like I was trying to explain to you a few minutes ago—that's honestly what finally got me in here to see you. Over these last few months, my mind just keeps jumping around so much, and it doesn't even matter if the room is dead silent. I could be sitting in the cab of my truck at two in the morning, nobody on the road, totally quiet, and my brain is still just ping-ponging all over the place. Like I said earlier, it’s every little CB chirp, or a fuel price sign out the window, or just some brand new idea that pops into my head about a sales route... it completely derails whatever I'm supposed to be looking at. 

You'd think a quiet room would make it easier to focus, right? Because there's less going on? But for me, it's almost worse. If there's nothing going on around me, my brain just makes up its own distractions. I'll try to read a manual or even just the newspaper, and I'll read the exact same paragraph six times in a row and not absorb a single word of it. And that's why I end up missing those details I normally never miss, like I was telling you—glossing over a client’s delivery note, or completely blanking on who I promised to call back. It’s all connected to this same issue where my focus is just... shot. Whether it's loud on the interstate or quiet in my living room, my attention span is just totally out the window right now.
Do you often have trouble keeping your workspace or living space organized?

Organized? Oh, no, not at all. I mean, if anything, I'm probably too organized. It's actually kind of a point of pride for me, to be honest. You see, when you're dealing with logistics and freight, organization isn't just some nice-to-have thing, it's the whole ballgame. If your paperwork is a mess, or if your cab looks like a bomb went off in it, you're going to lose a bill of lading, or you're going to miss a weigh station receipt, and then the whole chain just falls apart. 

So, no, my spaces are spotless. My truck cab? You could practically eat off the dashboard. I have a specific compartment for my logbooks, a specific folder for my receipts, and I wipe down the steering wheel and the gauges every single morning before I even turn the key.
